analysis.one_liner: Bans candy, fruit, and menthol flavors in e-cigarettes and cigars to curb youth vaping.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban flavored e-cigarettes and cigars died in committee; it was never voted on before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Kids Act would have banned characterizing flavors—including menthol, fruit, and candy flavors—in all tobacco products other than cigarettes, covering e-cigarettes, vape pens, cigars, and other non-cigarette products. E-cigarette makers could keep a flavor only if the FDA formally found it helps smokers quit, does not attract kids, and does not add harm. The bill cited government data showing youth e-cigarette use jumped 78% among high schoolers in 2018 and that 81% of kids who use tobacco started with a flavored product. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face far fewer flavored nicotine products designed to appeal to them, plus parents and schools dealing with youth vaping. Public health groups argue it would prevent kids from starting a lifetime nicotine addiction, since the bill cites data that flavors are a primary reason youth use e-cigarettes and cigars.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits characterizing flavors—strawberry, gummy bear, menthol, and more—in every tobacco product except cigarettes, removing the products the bill's findings say attract young users.

The bill's own findings state that youth e-cigarette use rose 78% among high school students and 48% among middle schoolers in 2018, reaching more than 3.6 million youth, and that both the Surgeon General and the FDA Commissioner called it an epidemic.

Citing survey data, the bill states 82% of current youth e-cigarette users said they used the products 'because they come in flavors I like,' and 81% of youth tobacco users started with a flavored product.
It would let a flavor stay on the market for an e-cigarette only if the FDA formally found it increases smoking cessation, does not increase youth initiation, and does not increase harm to users.

analysis.who_pays: E-cigarette and vape manufacturers, flavored cigar makers, and the retailers who sell their products would lose a large share of their market, since flavored products are the bulk of youth appeal. Some adult vapers and smokers who use flavors to stay off cigarettes would lose access unless the FDA approved a specific flavor for them.

drawbacks.text: Many adult smokers and vapers use flavored products to quit or avoid cigarettes; an outright ban would remove those options unless a manufacturer could meet the bill's high FDA-approval bar, which requires proving the flavor increases smoking cessation.

The ban covers all non-cigarette products but leaves flavored cigarettes untouched—menthol cigarettes, the most common flavored cigarette, would remain legal, a gap critics of flavor bans have long pointed out.
Banning flavors could push some users back to cigarettes, which public health authorities consider more harmful than vaping for adult smokers trying to switch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a real public health benefit—cutting off the flavored products that data show drive youth vaping—while the costs fall mainly on a specific industry and on some adults who rely on flavored products to quit smoking. The menthol-cigarette carve-out is a real weakness, but the bill's target, youth nicotine addiction, is a harm that falls on ordinary families. The main design question is whether the FDA exception process is workable in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee on March 5-6, 2019, and nothing further happened; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill with Rep. Jamie Raskin on March 5, 2019.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day and to the Subcommittee on Health the next day.
Thirty-three House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no action, hearing, or vote followed in the roughly two years before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: E-cigarette and vape companies and flavored cigar makers are better off, because a ban on the flavored products at the center of youth vaping never advanced. Kids and parents gained nothing from the bill's failure, and youth vaping policy instead moved later through separate regulatory channels outside this bill's record.

for.name: Rep. Diana DeGette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban flavored non-cigarette tobacco products.

for.name: Rep. Jamie Raskin
for.what_they_did: Joined DeGette in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action on it—no markup, no hearing, no floor vote—before the Congress ended.

against.name: E-cigarette and flavored tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers and sellers of flavored vape and cigar products
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in defeating flavor bans, which would remove the products driving youth use; the industry publicly campaigned against flavor restrictions during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were Democrats and there is no record of Republican support or opposition; the bill never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would have shown the parties' positions.

industries.note: Flavored products are the main driver of youth vaping and the core of the retail market; a ban would wipe out that segment, as the bill's own findings show 82% of youth users cite flavors as their reason for use.

industries.industry: Flavored cigar makers and convenience store retailers
industries.note: Flavored cigars made up more than half of the convenience store cigar market, and the bill bans those flavors; retailers profit from cheap flavored cigar sales that the bill's findings link to youth use.
The bill exempts FDA-approved therapeutic cessation products from the definition of e-cigarettes, keeping approved quitting aids available while flavored consumer products are removed.
